title: NULL, error handling and input validation
learningObjectives: Distinguish null, uninitialized, dangling and otherwise invalid pointers, and explain the limits of NULL checks.
Specify function contracts for nullable arguments, preconditions, success, failure and ownership.
Validate pointer arguments, numeric ranges, text conversions and library return values before use.
Choose error-reporting methods including status returns, output parameters, errno and stream indicators.
Design cleanup paths that release resources exactly once and preserve the primary failure.
Test normal, boundary and failure paths including null arguments, failed conversions, allocation and I/O errors.

understand.concept: A null pointer is a pointer value guaranteed not to compare equal to a pointer to any object or function. NULL is a macro for a null pointer constant and commonly represents an absent object reference. It is not the same as an uninitialized pointer, dangling pointer or arbitrary invalid address. Error handling defines observable success and failure outcomes; validation checks that values satisfy the contract before use.
understand.whyItMatters: C does not automatically check pointer validity, array bounds, numeric ranges, allocation success or I/O success. Explicit contracts and failure paths prevent invalid assumptions from becoming memory errors or corrupted data.
understand.analogy: Treat each function and allocation request as a contract with valid inputs, promised results and defined failure behaviour.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's rules for object lifetime, bounds, arithmetic or library contracts.

explain.narrative: Initialize pointers before use. A check that p is not NULL proves only that it is not null; it does not prove that p designates a live object of the correct type or that indexing is in bounds. Document whether pointer arguments may be NULL, the extent of arrays, mutation and ownership. Return a status when callers must decide what to do; use output parameters for results and specify whether they remain unchanged on failure. Validate external input at its boundary. Check scanf conversion counts or strtol end pointers and range, reject invalid lengths before indexing, and check allocation and I/O results. errno is meaningful only when the called function documents its use and its specified failure condition occurs. For streams, distinguish end-of-file from I/O failure with feof and ferror. Use staged cleanup so every acquired resource is released exactly once.

examples.title: Validated function with status result
examples.explanation: The function validates the output pointer and numeric preconditions before writing. The caller checks the status before using the output.

examples.title: Parse and range-check an integer
examples.explanation: strtol supplies an end pointer and reports range errors through errno. The function rejects empty input, no digits, trailing text and values outside int range; output is written only after all checks pass.

practise.guidedTask: Test percentage with valid 3/4, total zero, part greater than total and NULL output. State whether the output changes in each case.
practise.independentTask: Test percentage with valid 3/4, total zero, part greater than total and NULL output. State whether the output changes in each case. Add boundary and failure tests and explain the expected result for each.
hints: Validate inputs before dereferencing or indexing.
Check library return values and document failure behaviour.
Keep output parameters unchanged on failure when promised by the contract.
Release each acquired resource exactly once.
Test normal, boundary and failure paths.
A diagnostic or check proves only what its defined scope covers.

options: Only that p is not a null pointer value.
That p points to a live object.
That every index is in bounds.
questions.answer: Only that p is not a null pointer value.
questions.explanation: A non-null pointer may still be dangling, misaligned or outside its intended object's bounds.

questions.prompt: Why check out == NULL before writing through out?
options: To avoid dereferencing a null pointer when NULL is not permitted.
To convert it to an integer.
questions.answer: To avoid dereferencing a null pointer when NULL is not permitted.
questions.explanation: The function contract must permit or reject a null output pointer before writing through it.

options: Digit consumption, trailing characters and range error.
Only whether the result is nonzero.
questions.answer: Digit consumption, trailing characters and range error.
questions.explanation: The end pointer identifies no conversion and trailing text; errno can report range failure as documented.

options: When the function documents its use and its failure condition occurs.
questions.answer: When the function documents its use and its failure condition occurs.
questions.explanation: errno is not a universal error flag; inspect the function's specified result first.

questions.prompt: If unchanged output on failure is promised, what must happen?
options: The output remains unchanged on every failure path.
It is always set to zero.
questions.answer: The output remains unchanged on every failure path.
questions.explanation: Write the output only after validation and successful computation.
